Two developers run the same Claude Code task in the same repository at the same commit. For one, it follows the project's logging conventions. For the other, it uses a different logger and a different date format. Both have identical project files.

What is the most useful first diagnostic step?

options.text: Have the second developer paste the project's logging conventions into every prompt until the behaviour of the two environments matches.
options.explanation: This is a workaround. The underlying cause stays in place and will affect other behaviour.

options.text: Reinstall Claude Code on the second developer's machine.
options.explanation: Reinstalling does not change the configuration files that are probably causing the difference.

options.text: Report the behaviour as model non-determinism.
options.explanation: A consistent, systematic difference between two environments points to configuration, not to random variation.

options.text: Check which instruction and memory files are loaded in each session, including user-level configuration.
options.explanation: Correct. With identical project files, the likely difference is in what else is loaded, such as personal configuration. Inspecting what is in effect locates the cause directly.

questions.taskStatement: Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
questions.stem:
A claims-letter generator must include the correct claim number, amount and decision, all of which exist in structured data. It must also be empathetic and clear. At present one person reads 20 letters before each release.

Which TWO evaluation methods should be combined to give coverage at scale? (Select TWO)

options.text: A text-overlap score between each generated letter and one approved reference letter, as the measure of tone.
options.explanation: Good letters legitimately differ in wording, so overlap with one reference penalises acceptable variation and does not measure empathy.

options.text: A model-based grader that is asked whether the numbers in each letter "look right".
options.explanation: Exact values should be verified deterministically. A judgement about whether numbers look right is less reliable and costs more than a comparison.

options.text: Code-based checks that compare the claim number, amount and decision in each letter with the source data.
options.explanation: Correct. Facts that exist in structured data can be checked exactly and cheaply in code, across every letter.

options.text: Letter length in words, as a proxy for clarity.
options.explanation: Length has no dependable relationship to clarity.

options.text: A model-based grader with a written rubric for empathy and clarity, calibrated against human ratings on a sample.
options.explanation: Correct. Subjective qualities need judgement. A rubric-driven grader scales, and calibration against human ratings keeps it trustworthy.

questions.taskStatement: Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
questions.stem:
A games studio localises dialogue into 14 languages. The quality criteria are explicit: preserve meaning, fit a character limit, and match each character's voice guide. First drafts meet all criteria 70% of the time. When human linguists give feedback, the second draft is usually correct, so feedback measurably improves the output. The studio wants to reduce linguist time without losing quality.

Which orchestration pattern fits?

options.text: An evaluator-optimiser loop: one call translates, another checks the result against the criteria and returns feedback, up to a set limit.
options.explanation: Correct. The pattern fits when evaluation criteria are clear and iteration demonstrably improves results, both of which hold here. A limit and a human fallback bound cost and risk.

options.text: A router that sends each language to its own prompt.
options.explanation: Routing may help language-specific phrasing, but it adds no evaluation or feedback, which is what turns failing drafts into passing ones.

options.text: A single autonomous agent that holds all three criteria in its prompt and is free to keep rewriting the script until it judges the result to be good.
options.explanation: With no explicit evaluation step and no bound on iterations, cost is unpredictable and the criteria are not systematically checked.

options.text: Generate five candidate translations for each line and choose one at random.
options.explanation: More candidates without evaluation does not raise the chance that the chosen one meets the criteria.

questions.taskStatement: Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
questions.stem:
An assistant sends a 14,000-token prefix with every request: tool definitions, system instructions and a product catalogue that changes weekly. Prompt caching is enabled, but usage reports show almost no cache reads. The first line of the system prompt is "Current time:" followed by a timestamp accurate to the second. The static content follows it, and the user message comes last. Traffic is steady at several requests per second.

What should be changed?

options.text: Shorten the catalogue to its most frequently requested products, so that the prefix is smaller and cache hits become more likely.
options.explanation: Hits depend on the prefix being identical, not on its length. The changing timestamp would still break every match.

options.text: Move the timestamp into the tool definitions.
options.explanation: Tool definitions are part of the cached prefix too, so the prefix would still change on every request.

options.text: Move the timestamp, and any other per-request content, after the static content so that the prefix stays identical.
options.explanation: Correct. A cache hit needs an identical prefix. A value that changes every second near the top invalidates everything after it, so dynamic content belongs after the stable block.

options.text: Turn prompt caching off, since it is not producing savings.
options.explanation: This gives up a large saving that a simple reordering would unlock.

questions.taskStatement: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
questions.stem:
During requirements gathering for a customer-conversation assistant, Product asks for all transcripts to be kept for two years to improve the product. Legal states that transcripts must be deleted after 90 days. Security wants no transcripts stored outside the primary region. The engineering lead suggests "going with Product's request for now and sorting it out after launch".

How should the architect handle this?

options.text: Keep transcripts for 90 days in the primary region to satisfy Legal and Security, and give Product a two-year store of the same transcripts with names and account numbers removed.
options.explanation: Removing names and account numbers does not make free-text transcripts anonymous, so this still conflicts with Legal's 90-day rule. It also settles a cross-functional trade-off unilaterally instead of having the accountable owner decide.

options.text: Document the conflict and its implications, bring the stakeholders together so that the accountable owner can decide, and record the agreed requirement before the design proceeds.
options.explanation: Correct. Conflicting requirements must be surfaced and resolved by those with the authority to decide. Designing on an unresolved conflict leads to rework or non-compliance.

options.text: Implement Legal's 90 days quietly and tell Product after launch.
options.explanation: A unilateral choice avoids the alignment that is needed and leaves Product's underlying need unexamined. That need might be met in another way, such as with anonymised data.

options.text: Follow the engineering lead's suggestion.
options.explanation: The system would launch in conflict with a stated legal requirement, with a retention design that is expensive to reverse.

questions.taskStatement: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
questions.stem:
A utility company launches an assistant intended to resolve billing queries end to end. The business goals are to resolve at least 60% of queries without a human, never to give incorrect tariff information, to respond within 5 seconds, and to stay under $0.04 per conversation. The team proposes to track only "average response length" and "messages per day".

Which set of metrics should be defined?

options.text: Outcome-verified resolution rate, graded accuracy of tariff answers, p95 latency, cost per conversation and policy-violation rate.
options.explanation: Correct. Each metric maps to a stated goal and covers the dimensions that matter: quality, latency, cost and safety.

options.text: The share of conversations that receive a thumbs-up.
options.explanation: Ratings come from a small, self-selected group of users and say nothing about tariff accuracy, latency or cost.

options.text: Text-overlap scores between each answer and an approved reference answer, together with messages per day and average response length.
options.explanation: Overlap with a reference wording measures neither factual correctness nor resolution, and message volume is activity, not outcome.

options.text: Average latency and service uptime.
options.explanation: These are operational measures only. An assistant can be fast, available and wrong.

questions.taskStatement: Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
questions.stem:
An architect must ask the chief financial officer to choose between three options for a document-processing system. Option 1 uses the smallest model: 91% accuracy at $8,000 a month. Option 2 uses routing: 96% at $19,000 a month. Option 3 uses the most capable model throughout: 97% at $52,000 a month. Each percentage point of error costs about $3,000 a month in manual rework. The CFO has ten minutes and no technical background.

How should the decision be presented?

options.text: By presenting only option 3, as "the most accurate", to keep the choice simple.
options.explanation: This withholds the alternatives and recommends the option with the highest total cost.

options.text: By sending the raw evaluation spreadsheets and letting the CFO draw conclusions.
options.explanation: This hands the analysis to the person least equipped to do it and offers no recommendation.

options.text: As a one-page comparison of each option's total monthly cost including rework, with the main risks and a clear recommendation.
options.explanation: Correct. With rework included, the totals are about $35,000, $31,000 and $61,000. Expressing the trade-off in the decision-maker's terms, with a recommendation, lets a non-technical executive decide quickly.

options.text: As a detailed walkthrough of model architectures, token pricing and benchmark methods, so that the CFO can verify the accuracy figures independently.
options.explanation: The CFO has neither the time nor the need for technical detail. The decision turns on total cost and risk.

questions.taskStatement: Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
questions.stem:
Field technicians ask an assistant questions such as "What does error E-4471 mean on the HX-200 pump?" The knowledge base is indexed with dense embeddings only. Conceptual questions, such as why a pump cavitates, are answered well. Queries containing exact error codes or part numbers often retrieve documents about different codes that are semantically similar.

Which retrieval strategy fits this query pattern?

options.text: A request that technicians describe errors in words instead of quoting codes.
options.explanation: This puts the burden on users and throws away the most precise identifier available.

options.text: Embeddings with a larger number of dimensions.
options.explanation: Higher-dimensional embeddings still represent meaning. They do not provide exact matching of codes.

options.text: Hybrid retrieval that combines keyword search with embedding search and merges or reranks the results.
options.explanation: Correct. Lexical search matches exact identifiers and embeddings capture meaning. Combining them serves both kinds of query.

options.text: Keyword search only, replacing the embeddings.
options.explanation: This fixes the code lookups but loses the conceptual matching that currently works well.

questions.taskStatement: Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
questions.stem:
A team builds a system to refactor a tightly coupled 4,000-line module. Any change to the data model affects the serialiser, the validators and the tests. Their design assigns four subagents (model, serialiser, validators, tests) that work in parallel, each in its own context, and merges their output at the end. The merged result repeatedly fails because the subagents make incompatible assumptions about field names and types. The whole module fits comfortably in one context window.

What should the architect change?

options.text: Let the four subagents message each other directly whenever they are unsure of a field name or type, and agree a value before continuing.
options.explanation: Peer-to-peer coordination adds overhead and still gives no guarantee of a consistent shared state. It is a complicated way to imitate a single context.

options.text: Add a fifth "merge" subagent that reconciles the incompatible outputs.
options.explanation: This repairs, after the fact, conflicts that the design itself creates. The incompatible assumptions arise from isolated contexts and will keep arising.

options.text: Run each subagent on a more capable model.
options.explanation: The failure comes from context isolation, not capability. Stronger models in separate contexts still cannot see one another's decisions.

options.text: Use a single agent that holds the whole module in context, and keep multi-agent designs for independent subtasks.
options.explanation: Correct. Parallel subagents suit separable work. Tightly coupled changes need shared context, and since the module fits in one window there is no reason to split it.

questions.taskStatement: Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)
questions.stem:
To cut costs, a team moved its contract-analysis assistant from the most capable model to the smallest. Overall accuracy fell from 93% to 86%. By category: clause extraction went from 97% to 96%, date and party identification stayed at 98%, and multi-clause reasoning (for example, "does clause 14 override the cap in clause 9?") fell from 84% to 52%. Reasoning questions are 22% of traffic. The prompts are unchanged.

What is the correct diagnosis and response?

options.text: The smallest model is mismatched to the reasoning category. Route those questions to the more capable model and keep the smallest model for the rest.
options.explanation: Correct. The category breakdown localises the loss to multi-step reasoning. Routing restores quality where it fell and keeps the saving on the 78% of traffic that was unaffected.

options.text: Retrieval is failing. Retrieve more clauses for every question.
options.explanation: Extraction and identification remain accurate, so the clauses are being found. The weakness is in reasoning across them.

options.text: The smallest model needs different prompting. Add worked examples of multi-clause reasoning to the prompt for every question and keep all traffic on the smallest model.
options.explanation: Examples might narrow the gap, but a 32-point drop on one category with unchanged prompts points to a capability mismatch, and examples on every request add cost to the 78% of traffic that does not need them.

options.text: The change failed. Move all traffic back to the most capable model.
options.explanation: This gives up the saving on the three-quarters of traffic where the smallest model performs equally well.

questions.taskStatement: Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
questions.stem:
A finance assistant drafts variance commentary. It is asked to total 140 ledger lines and compute percentage variances. Reviewers find totals that are off by small amounts in about 3% of reports, although the narrative is good. The reports go to auditors.

How should the architect address this failure mode?

options.text: Carry out the calculations in deterministic code, exposed as a tool, and have the model write the commentary around the computed figures.
options.explanation: Correct. Language models are unreliable at exact arithmetic over long lists. Deterministic computation removes the failure mode and leaves the model the part it does well.

options.text: Round every figure in the report to the nearest thousand, so that small discrepancies in totals and variances are no longer visible to reviewers or auditors.
options.explanation: This conceals the errors instead of removing them and makes the report less precise.

options.text: Use a more capable model for the arithmetic.
options.explanation: The error rate may fall but exactness is still not guaranteed, and auditors require exact figures.

options.text: Instruct the model to double-check its sums before answering.
options.explanation: The check is done by the same mechanism that made the error, so some errors will remain.

questions.taskStatement: Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)
questions.stem:
Over three months a team appended 14 rules to a support assistant's system prompt, each one fixing a reported problem. No evaluation was run after any edit. The assistant now refuses legitimate refund requests: rule 9 says "never promise refunds", while rule 3 says "process refunds under $50 immediately". Its greetings have also become oddly formal. The model and tools are unchanged.

What should the team do?

options.text: The accumulated rules conflict. Build a regression suite, consolidate the prompt to resolve the contradictions, and run the suite on every change.
options.explanation: Correct. This is prompt failure through unmanaged accretion. Fixing it takes both a coherent prompt and tests that catch regressions when it changes.

options.text: Add a fifteenth rule at the top of the prompt: "When any of the rules below appear to conflict, use common sense to decide which one applies."
options.explanation: This leaves the contradictions in place and asks the model to guess which rule the business intends.

options.text: Move to a different model.
options.explanation: The contradiction is in the prompt. Any model given both rules faces the same conflict.

options.text: Restore the prompt from three months ago.
options.explanation: This brings back the 14 problems that the rules were written to fix.
